objectives: Recognize the major equine emergencies (colic, laminitis, EHV).
Manage the canonical bovine + swine + small-ruminant diseases.
Apply Radostits-style herd-health + welfare frameworks (Grandin handling, dairy + feedlot).

slides.title: Equine medicine: colic, laminitis, EHV + the structure of equine emergency practice
slides.body:
The horse (Equus caballus) is uniquely vulnerable to GI catastrophe + lower-limb crisis. ~10% of horses experience colic in any given year + colic remains the #1 medical cause of equine death in most surveys.

**Equine colic** — abdominal pain — is a syndrome with many causes, classified by anatomic location + mechanism:
- **Spasmodic / gas colic**: mild + transient; responds to NSAIDs + spasmolytics.
- **Impaction**: dehydrated ingesta in pelvic flexure, transverse colon, or cecum. IV fluids + oral fluids via NG tube + repeated rectals.
- **Displacement**: large colon left dorsal displacement (LDDD/nephrosplenic entrapment), right dorsal displacement, 180° volvulus. Surgical risk variable.
- **Strangulating**: small intestinal volvulus, pedunculated lipoma (older horses — common), inguinal hernia, intussusception, epiploic foramen entrapment. **Surgical emergency** — survival depends on early referral.
- **Enteritis + colitis**: proximal enteritis (anterior duodenitis-jejunitis), Salmonella colitis, *Clostridium difficile*, right dorsal colitis (NSAID-induced), Potomac horse fever (*Neorickettsia risticii*).

**Workup**: pain assessment (Horse Grimace Scale), HR (>60 ominous), CRT, mucous membranes, dehydration, nasogastric reflux (>2 L = small-intestinal lesion), rectal palpation (gas distension, displacement, masses), abdominal ultrasound (FLASH — Fast Localized Abdominal Sonography of Horses), abdominocentesis (TP + lactate — >4 mmol/L peritoneal lactate worrisome), serum lactate + PCV/TP. **Decision point**: medical vs. referral surgical — call early. Survival of strangulating SI lesions ~50-70% with early surgery vs. ~0% without.

**Laminitis** — inflammation + structural failure of the lamellae attaching the third phalanx (P3) to the hoof wall. Three classic syndromes (van Eps + Pollitt 2014):
1. **Endotoxin/sepsis-associated** (carbohydrate overload, colitis, RFM/retained placenta, sepsis) — the historical 'classic' laminitis.
2. **Endocrinopathic** — equine metabolic syndrome (EMS — insulin resistance, obesity) + PPID (pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction = Cushing's, older horses, treated with pergolide). **Most common cause in modern practice** — UC Davis + UQ Pollitt + Donnelly studies.
3. **Supporting-limb laminitis** — contralateral overload during prolonged non-weight-bearing (Barbaro 2007 high-profile case).

Signs: bilateral forelimb 'sawhorse stance', heat in hooves, bounding digital pulses, reluctance to move, pain on hoof testers, eventually rotation + sinking of P3 on radiographs. Treatment: aggressive cryotherapy (ice the entire distal limb for prevention in at-risk cases — UQ Pollitt + van Eps); analgesia (NSAIDs, opioids, lidocaine CRI, gabapentin); mechanical hoof support (frog support, deep bedding, custom shoeing — heart-bar, glue-on, clog); address the underlying endocrine or septic cause; long convalescence. Prognosis guarded.

**Equine herpesvirus (EHV-1, EHV-4)**:
- **EHV-1**: respiratory + abortion + neurologic (equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy, EHM — vasculitis + spinal cord ischemia). Recent outbreaks (Valencia 2021, US dressage circuit) cause biosecurity scrambles. PCR on nasopharyngeal swab + blood. Strict isolation + biosecurity + supportive care. Vaccine reduces respiratory + abortion forms but does NOT prevent EHM.
- **EHV-4**: respiratory disease + occasional abortion.

Other equine clinical priorities: **strangles** (*Streptococcus equi equi*; abscessing lymphadenopathy; quarantine + ELISA SeM titer + culture); **EIA** (Equine Infectious Anemia, Coggins test); **West Nile virus + EEE/WEE/VEE** (vaccines core); **rabies** (core vaccine; the only zoonotic vaccine-preventable horse disease); **recurrent airway obstruction (RAO/heaves)**; **exercise-induced pulmonary hemorrhage (EIPH)**; **recurrent laryngeal neuropathy** ('roaring' — surgical tie-back/laryngoplasty).

slides.title: Bovine medicine + dairy industry: mastitis, ketosis, milk fever, brucellosis
slides.body:
Dairy + beef cattle are the backbone of food-animal practice. **Radostits, Gay, Hinchcliff, Constable** — *Veterinary Medicine: A Textbook of the Diseases of Cattle, Horses, Sheep, Pigs and Goats* (11th ed. 2017) — is the canonical large-animal IM reference, the equivalent of Ettinger for production species.

**Mastitis** — inflammation of the mammary gland — the #1 economic disease of dairy cattle (USD ~$2 billion/yr in US losses). **Etiology + classification**:
- **Contagious** (cow-to-cow at milking): *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus agalactiae*, *Mycoplasma*. Spread by milkers' hands + milking unit.
- **Environmental** (from bedding, soil, manure): *E. coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Streptococcus uberis*, *Streptococcus dysgalactiae*, *Enterococcus*.
- **Clinical**: visible abnormal milk + udder swelling + ± systemic signs.
- **Subclinical**: only somatic cell count elevation (>200,000/mL); the iceberg under clinical cases.

**Diagnosis**: California Mastitis Test (CMT — cowside SCC screen), bulk-tank + individual SCC, milk culture (selective + chromogenic media + PCR), serology (Mycoplasma, Staph aureus). **Treatment**: intramammary + systemic antibiotics for clinical (e.g., ceftiofur, pirlimycin, amoxicillin-clavulanate); selective dry-cow therapy (no longer blanket — antibiotic stewardship); culling chronic Staph aureus + Mycoplasma cows; **milk withdrawal times** strictly observed (residue avoidance — FDA/FARAD). Prevention: 5-point Cow + udder hygiene + dipping + drying + dry-cow therapy + culling — the **NMC (National Mastitis Council) Five-Point Plan**.

**Ketosis + negative energy balance + the transition cow**:
- Early lactation, peak milk output exceeds dry-matter intake → **negative energy balance** → mobilization of body fat → ketone-body production (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, acetone).
- **Type 1**: classic lactational; cow off feed, weight loss, decreased milk, sweet/acetone breath, sometimes nervous signs.
- **Type 2**: fatty-liver-associated, often with retained placenta + metritis + LDA.
- **Subclinical ketosis** (BHB 1.2-2.9 mmol/L) is widespread + costs heavily in production losses.
- **Diagnosis**: cowside BHB meter (KetoTest, Precision Xtra), urine ketones; herd-level Ketolac/MUN screening.
- **Treatment**: oral propylene glycol (50% dextrose IV is short-lived — propylene glycol is the workhorse); B12 + dexamethasone; nutritional management (transition cow nutrition — UW Drackley + Cornell van Saun + others have developed the modern transition-cow framework).

**Milk fever (parturient paresis / hypocalcemia)**:
- Periparturient cow (typically within 48 h of calving) with hypocalcemia (iCa <0.8 mmol/L) → muscle weakness, recumbency, depression, hypothermia, dilated pupils, GI stasis. Classic three stages from mild restlessness to lateral recumbency.
- **Treatment**: slow IV calcium borogluconate (one 500-mL bottle of 23% Ca borogluconate over 10-20 min; auscultate heart for arrhythmia; have epinephrine ready). Most cows respond visibly within minutes.
- **Prevention**: DCAD (dietary cation-anion difference) diets in late dry period — negative DCAD induces a mild metabolic acidosis that primes Ca mobilization; oral Ca boluses at calving for high-risk cows.

**Other bovine priorities**:
- **Displaced abomasum (LDA)**: gas-filled abomasum displaces under rumen to left flank; 'ping' on auscultation-percussion. Roll-and-toggle, right-flank omentopexy, or right paramedian abomasopexy — surgical correction routine.
- **BRD (Bovine Respiratory Disease)**: feedlot + calf pneumonia complex — *Mannheimia haemolytica*, *Pasteurella multocida*, *Histophilus somni*, *Mycoplasma bovis*; viral primers (BHV-1/IBR, BVDV, BRSV, PI3, bovine coronavirus). Mass treatment + metaphylactic antibiotics + vaccines + Frank Hurtig + Booker era research.
- **BVDV**: persistent infection (PI) animals shed virus throughout life; test + cull PI calves.
- **Reproductive**: dystocia, retained placenta, metritis, ovarian cysts, embryo loss; OvSynch + reproductive-management protocols (Pursley + Wiltbank Wisconsin).
- **Foot disease**: digital dermatitis (treponemes), sole ulcer, white-line disease — major welfare + production issue.

**Brucellosis** — *Brucella abortus* (cattle), *B. melitensis* (sheep + goats), *B. suis* (swine), *B. canis* (dogs). **Zoonotic**: undulant fever in humans. **Eradication programs** (US Bangs program) have largely eliminated *B. abortus* from US cattle (final reservoir in Greater Yellowstone bison + elk — controversy with NPS + ranchers). Mandatory test + slaughter + ring-test surveillance + vaccination (RB51 calfhood vaccine in many states). Importation of breeding cattle from non-eradicated countries requires testing.

slides.title: Swine + small ruminants + welfare: Temple Grandin + the modern production framework
slides.body:
**Swine medicine** — vertically-integrated industry; vet often serves a system (Smithfield, JBS, Tyson, Seaboard) more than individual farms.
- **PRRS (Porcine Reproductive + Respiratory Syndrome)**: arterivirus; abortion storms + nursery pneumonia; vaccines + biosecurity + 'load-close-expose' acclimation protocols.
- **Porcine epidemic diarrhea (PED)**: coronavirus; devastating 2013-2014 US outbreak killed ~7M piglets.
- **Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae**: enzootic pneumonia; subclinical losses; vaccines.
- **Swine influenza A**: H1N1, H1N2, H3N2; zoonotic + reverse-zoonotic potential — the 2009 H1N1 pandemic emerged in pigs.
- **African swine fever (ASF)**: hemorrhagic DNA virus; spread from Africa to Eastern Europe + Asia (China 2018+ — devastating); not yet in US but #1 perceived threat. No vaccine licensed in most regions until ~2023 (Vietnam approval).
- **PCV2 + PMWS**: porcine circovirus; vaccine highly effective + transformed nursery health.
- **Welfare**: gestation crates phased out in EU + some US states (Prop 12 California 2018, in effect 2024+ litigation); group housing alternatives.

**Small ruminants — sheep + goats**:
- **Parasitism + anthelmintic resistance**: *Haemonchus contortus* (barber-pole worm) is the #1 sheep + goat killer in warm-moist climates; widespread resistance to benzimidazoles, levamisole, macrocyclic lactones. **FAMACHA** (eyelid color score; Faffa Malan, South Africa) targeted-selective treatment is the modern standard; refugia + larval drying + species rotation.
- **CAE (caprine arthritis-encephalitis) + OPP (ovine progressive pneumonia)**: lentiviruses; lifelong infection; test-and-cull eradication.
- **Caseous lymphadenitis**: *Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis*; abscesses; vaccine + biosecurity.
- **Foot rot**: *Dichelobacter nodosus* + *Fusobacterium necrophorum*.
- **Pregnancy toxemia / ketosis** in late-gestation does/ewes carrying multiples; metabolic crisis like dairy cow.
- **Coccidiosis** in lambs/kids; coccidiostats in creep feed.
- **Tetanus, enterotoxemia (overeating disease, *Clostridium perfringens* type D)** — core vaccine.
- **Goat polio + listeriosis + urinary calculi (urolithiasis)** in wethers.

**Camelids (llamas, alpacas)** — increasingly relevant; meningeal worm (Parelaphostrongylus tenuis), heat stress, mineral imbalances; obstetrics; clinical similarity to ruminants but enough difference to warrant species-specific texts (Cebra + Anderson).

**Production-medicine framework + welfare**:
- **Herd-health approach**: vet thinks population-level — incidence, prevalence, days-open, calf mortality, SCC, mastitis-cure-rate, breed-back-rate, weaning rate, mortality, treatment frequency. Use **records** (DairyComp 305, PigChamp, FarmWizard, vet practice software) for surveillance.
- **Five Freedoms (FAWC 1979)**: freedom from hunger/thirst, discomfort, pain/injury/disease, fear/distress, + freedom to express normal behavior. Foundation of modern welfare assessment.
- **Five Domains model (David Mellor, Massey University, 2015+)**: extends to mental state + positive welfare — covered in detail in the modern-frontier lesson.

**Temple Grandin** (Colorado State University; b. 1947) revolutionized livestock handling through her autistic-perspective insights into animal vision + flight zone + point-of-balance:
- **Curved handling systems** (single-file races, solid walls so cattle see only the path ahead, no shadows + glints + distractions). Designed for major US + global beef + dairy operations.
- **Center-track restrainer** + **double-rail conveyor** for slaughter — humane stunning standards.
- **Audited scoring system** for slaughter plants (% stunned on first shot, % falling, % vocalizations, % electric prod use) — adopted by AMI + McDonald's + Wendy's + Walmart supplier audits + transformed industry.
- *Animals in Translation* (2005), *Humane Livestock Handling* (2008), *Thinking in Pictures* (1995) — Grandin's books are required reading. Grandin's influence on humane slaughter + handling design is the single most significant welfare-engineering contribution of the modern era.

Production medicine = **animal health + welfare + economics + public health + One Health** integrated. The food-animal veterinarian is at once a clinician, epidemiologist, nutritionist, welfare advocate, + economic adviser — a profile that Radostits' textbook captures exactly.

question.question: Triage a colicking horse + decide medical vs. surgical referral
question.goal: Apply equine colic assessment to a Quarter Horse gelding with 4 h of pain.

steps.prompt: On arrival: HR 72, restless + pawing, mucous membranes injected, CRT 3 s, PCV 52%, TP 8.5. What does the bloodwork picture suggest?

acceptedAnswers: hemoconcentration + dehydration + early endotoxemia/shock — significant systemic compromise
PCV/TP both elevated → dehydration; tachycardia + injected MM → systemic compromise

steps.reveal: PCV 52% (elevated) + TP 8.5 (elevated) = **hemoconcentration** from dehydration ± splenic contraction. HR 72 in a colicking horse is concerning (>60 ominous; >80 grave). Injected MM + CRT 3 s = early systemic compromise / endotoxemia. This horse needs urgent fluid resuscitation + decision about referral.

steps.prompt: Nasogastric intubation yields 8 L of foul reflux. What does that mean + what does it not mean?

acceptedAnswers: significant small-intestinal disease — proximal enteritis or small-intestinal strangulating obstruction; cannot distinguish medical from surgical without further workup

steps.reveal: **>2 L gastric reflux = small-intestinal lesion**: either **proximal enteritis (anterior duodenitis-jejunitis, PE)** — typically medical with prolonged NG decompression + IV fluids + lidocaine CRI — OR **small-intestinal strangulating obstruction** (volvulus, pedunculated lipoma, epiploic foramen entrapment) — surgical. **Cannot distinguish on reflux alone**. Need rectal + ultrasound + abdominocentesis + serial assessment. **Decompress horse via NG tube** + buy time.

steps.prompt: Rectal: distended loops of small intestine palpable. Abdominal ultrasound: distended SI loops, amotile, with thick wall. Abdominocentesis: clear yellow fluid, TP 3.5 g/dL, lactate 2.5 mmol/L. Surgical or medical?

acceptedAnswers: borderline — distended amotile SI is concerning for strangulation; serial assessment + early referral are warranted; peritoneal fluid currently not strongly abnormal but can lag
concerning for strangulating SI lesion → referral with surgical option ready

steps.reveal: Distended amotile SI loops on rectal + ultrasound = **strangulation suspected** until proven otherwise. Peritoneal lactate is **early-stage normal** in this horse but can rise rapidly with bowel compromise; **peritoneal fluid TP + lactate > systemic lactate suggests strangulation**. **Refer immediately**. Survival of strangulating SI lesions ~70-85% with surgery within 6-8 h of onset; falls dramatically with each hour of delay. Continue NG decompression, IV fluids (10-20 mL/kg/h initially), analgesia, monitoring during transport.

steps.prompt: Owner asks: 'can we just keep treating medically — maybe it will resolve?' What is your discussion?

acceptedAnswers: discuss prognosis — strangulating lesion will not resolve medically; delay reduces survival; cost ~$10-15k; humane euthanasia if surgery declined
explain that strangulating lesions require surgery; declining surgery typically means humane euthanasia is the appropriate next step

hints: What is the alternative if surgery declined?
steps.reveal: **Honest communication**: a strangulating SI lesion will not resolve medically. Continued conservative management = ongoing pain + necrotic bowel + endotoxemia + death (typically 12-48 h, painful). **Options**: (1) emergency referral for exploratory celiotomy — cost USD 8-15k typical; survival 70-85% if operated <8 h, lower with delay or compromise of long bowel segments; (2) **humane euthanasia** — appropriate if surgery declined or prognosis poor. Equine clients respect honest framing of these decisions. **Document** the discussion in the record + obtain informed consent or DNR. The veterinarian's job is to lay out the options + the realistic prognosis + then support the owner's decision — not to make it for them.

question.question: Why is Temple Grandin's design work considered the single most important welfare-engineering contribution to modern livestock production?
options: Temple Grandin (Colorado State, b. 1947) used her autistic-perspective sensory insight into cattle vision + flight zone + point-of-balance to redesign the **physical infrastructure** of livestock handling + slaughter: curved single-file races with solid walls (cattle see only the path ahead, not handlers or shadows or distractions), center-track conveyor restrainers for slaughter, double-rail systems, + non-slip flooring. She then created **audited scoring systems** for slaughter plants — % stunned on first shot, % falling, % vocalizing, % electric-prod use — that McDonald's + Wendy's + Walmart adopted for supplier audits. Within a decade, US slaughter-plant performance scores transformed industry-wide. Her books — *Animals in Translation*, *Humane Livestock Handling*, *Thinking in Pictures* — became standard references. The genius is that she translated welfare from a **moral exhortation** into a **measurable, designable, audit-able engineering practice**. Grandin's curved races are now the global standard. No single person has had more practical effect on animal welfare in production agriculture in the modern era — combining empathy, engineering, autism-perspective sensory understanding, + corporate-audit institutional design.
question.explanation: Temple Grandin combined autistic-perspective sensory insight, engineering design (curved races, center-track restrainers, solid-wall single-file systems), + corporate audit systems (McDonald's/Walmart supplier audits) to transform livestock handling + slaughter welfare. She translated welfare from moral exhortation into measurable engineering practice. Her global design standards + books are the most important welfare-engineering contribution of the modern era.

slides.workedSolution: Temple Grandin used autistic-perspective sensory understanding of cattle vision + flight zone to design curved handling systems + center-track restrainers + audit scoring systems adopted by McDonald's/Walmart. She translated welfare from moral claim into measurable engineering practice. Her books + global standards make her the most important welfare-engineering contributor of the modern era.

question.question: A 600-cow dairy reports a spike in cases of left displaced abomasum + retained placentae + mastitis over the past month. Apply Radostits-style herd-health + transition-cow analysis.
question.scenario: Apply production-medicine framework to a multifactorial herd problem.
question.modelAnswer: **The pattern points to transition-cow dysfunction**. LDA + retained placenta + mastitis + ketosis + metritis cluster within 21 d of calving — the **'transition period' (3 wk pre-calving to 3 wk post-calving)** is the highest-risk window in a dairy cow's life + the diagnostic anchor for herd-level investigation (Drackley, Overton, van Saun). **Approach**: (1) **Define the problem** — pull DairyComp records: incidence rates per 100 calvings, age + parity distribution, calving season, sire effects, days-in-milk at diagnosis, treatment costs, milk-yield + cull patterns. (2) **Transition cow audit** (van Saun + Sniffen): assess pre-fresh + fresh pen nutrition (DCAD diet in pre-fresh? negative-DCAD targeted to mobilize Ca; NEL adequate? CP + amino acid balance? forage:concentrate ratio? particle size + sorting?), stocking density (≥30 inches of bunk space, ≥1 stall per cow), heat stress (THI + fans + sprinklers + shade), social grouping (avoid pen moves <3 wk pre-calving), water access. (3) **Subclinical ketosis screening** — herd-level BHB on a cohort of fresh cows (target <15% with BHB >1.2 mmol/L); MUN; body-condition-score tracking (target dry-off ~3.25-3.5 + maintain through calving). (4) **Mastitis audit** — bulk tank SCC trend + cultures, individual SCC + new-infection rate, dry-cow + lactating mastitis treatment + cure rate, milking-procedure observation (pre-dip → forestrip → wipe → unit attach within 60-90 s of stimulation → post-dip), liner condition, vacuum + pulsation, NMC Five-Point Plan compliance. (5) **Surgery + treatment audit** — LDA repair technique + cure rate; cesarean + RP management; metritis treatment protocol (ceftiofur per FDA-approved 2-shot regimen, no oxytetracycline IU). (6) **Intervention** — refine transition-cow diet + management; add monensin (Rumensin) if appropriate per regional + welfare regulations; targeted dry-cow therapy; oral Ca boluses for older cows at calving; oral propylene glycol or monensin for ketosis prevention; consider negative-DCAD anionic salts; staff training on milking hygiene + standard operating procedures. (7) **Monitor** — recheck incidence in 3-6 mo. **Radostits-style herd health** treats the dairy as a single integrated system; the LDA + RP + mastitis cluster is almost always a transition-management diagnosis at the herd level, not a coincidence at the individual-cow level.
question.rubric: Identifies the transition-cow period, uses Radostits/Drackley/van Saun framework, audits nutrition (DCAD, energy, particle size), stocking + heat stress, mastitis Five-Point Plan, ketosis surveillance, intervention + monitoring; demonstrates herd-level production-medicine thinking + uses records as the diagnostic substrate.

question.question: A dairy herd has 600 lactating cows, bulk-tank SCC = 320,000/mL. Target is ≤200,000/mL. Approximately what proportion of the herd is likely infected, + what is the production cost? (Use rule of thumb: each 100,000 SCC above 100,000 → ~1.5 kg milk loss per cow per day.)
acceptedAnswers: 320 above baseline 100 by 220 → loss ≈ 1.5 × 2.2 ≈ 3.3 kg/cow/day; herd loss ≈ 3.3 × 600 ≈ 1980 kg/day; ~30-40% subclinically infected
~3.3 kg/cow/day milk loss × 600 cows = ~2000 kg/day; ~30% infected estimated
question.explanation: Bulk-tank SCC 320k is well above 200k target. Rule of thumb (Hortet + Seegers; NMC): each 100k above ~100k baseline costs ~1.5 kg milk per cow per day. 320 − 100 = 220k above baseline → 2.2 × 1.5 ≈ **3.3 kg lost per cow per day**. For 600 cows: ~**2000 kg/day = ~$700/day at ~$0.35/kg milk price** in production loss alone — not counting treatment, discarded milk, antibiotic stewardship, culls, premium incentives. Roughly **30-40%** of cows are typically subclinically infected at this SCC level. Investigate via individual SCC, milk culture, milking-procedure audit + NMC Five-Point Plan + selective dry-cow therapy. The math itself is a Radostits-style production-medicine economic argument that converts SCC into dollars + drives owner engagement.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why production-medicine veterinarians think at the herd level rather than the individual-animal level, + name one major welfare-engineering contribution.
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) Production-medicine practice (Radostits et al.) treats the dairy/feedlot/swine farm/sheep flock as a single integrated economic + biological system — incidence rates, SCC, mortality, days-open, cull patterns, mastitis cure, transition-cow audit, herd-health visits + records — rather than individual sick-animal medicine. (2) Reason: most herd losses are subclinical + multifactorial (nutrition, management, biosecurity, stocking, ventilation) + cannot be solved one cow at a time. (3) Veterinarian role: epidemiologist + nutritionist + welfare adviser + economic analyst. (4) Welfare engineering: Temple Grandin's curved races + center-track restrainers + audited slaughter scoring transformed industry practice via measurable design, not exhortation; FAWC Five Freedoms + Mellor Five Domains frameworks structure assessment. Concludes that production medicine = integrated population-level practice combining animal health, welfare, public health, + economics.
